slides: Open by shifting attention from a single waveform to a family of stationary processes. The chapter treats a signal as a point on a statistical manifold whose geometry can be inspected through autocovariance, spectrum, and finite-dimensional linear-system coordinates rather than by staring at one trace.

Use the route slide to orient the sparse artifact set. The dashboard supplies the durable static picture, the AR one spectral surface is the interactive companion, and the sanity checks certify that the examples satisfy stationarity, positive spectrum, autocorrelation decay, and positive semidefinite covariance.

Stationarity is the first geometric reduction. Once moments depend only on lag, the signal is represented by an autocovariance sequence or equivalently by a spectral density. The dashboard makes this move visible by pairing time-domain and frequency-domain summaries of the same process family.

The AR one example is the classroom anchor. A single parameter controls both geometric position and decay rate, while the stationarity boundary remains visible at absolute phi equal one. The sanity margin of 0.3 records that the displayed parameter stays safely inside the stable region.

The spectral surface slide explains why the interactive artifact exists. Moving phi changes how power concentrates across frequencies, so the model family is a surface of positive spectra rather than just a line of time traces. Positivity is part of the statistical geometry.

Autocovariance positive semidefiniteness is a quiet but essential check. A sequence of lag covariances is not valid merely because it looks smooth; every finite Toeplitz covariance matrix must be positive semidefinite. This is the finite-dimensional shadow of spectral nonnegativity.

Linear systems enter as finite-dimensional submanifolds inside the larger space of stationary processes. Coefficients, transfer functions, and innovation variance give coordinates, but the statistical object is still the induced distribution over signals. The diagram keeps the system-to-spectrum pipeline explicit.

This slide distinguishes coordinate systems from the underlying process. AR, MA, and ARMA descriptions can emphasize different sides of the same stationary family. Information geometry asks which coordinates reveal stable inference directions and which simply reparameterize the same spectral behavior.

The sanity checks are useful because polished plots can hide invalid time-series examples. Here the AR autocorrelation decays, autocovariance matrices are positive semidefinite, spectra remain positive, and the stationarity margin is explicit. That makes the dashboard safe to teach from.

Close by tying the chapter to the previous inference material. Time-series models are not outside information geometry; they are statistical manifolds with dependence structure. Linear systems provide low-dimensional coordinates, spectra provide observable geometry, and sanity checks keep those coordinates honest.
